subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Korean Tea Traditions
description: A short lesson to help you apply Korean Tea Traditions.

hook.text: Korea's tea tradition dates to the 7th century, when Buddhist monks brought seeds from Tang China.

buildup.text: Korean tea culture emphasizes simplicity and nature. Pots are earthy, cups are small, settings are calm.

discovery.text: The 'dado' ceremony focuses on mindfulness, not rigid choreography. It's more relaxed than Japan's form.

twist.text: Korea's tea culture nearly vanished during the Joseon Dynasty when Confucianism replaced Buddhism.

climax.text: A revival began in the 20th century. Today, Korean green tea from Boseong is internationally celebrated.

punchline.text: A tradition that nearly died is thriving once more.

quiz.question: Why did Korean tea culture nearly disappear?
options: Confucianism replaced Buddhism during the Joseon Dynasty

details.summary: Korea received tea culture from China during the Three Kingdoms period. Korean tea culture emphasizes simplicity and natural beauty. Darye, the Korean tea ceremony, is less formal than Japan's but equally meditative.
details.whyItMatters: Korean tea culture bridges Chinese and Japanese traditions while maintaining its own identity. Its modern revival shows how cultures can reconnect with forgotten heritage.
takeaways: Korea received tea from China during the Three Kingdoms era
Darye is the Korean tea ceremony emphasizing simplicity
Korean tea culture has experienced a strong modern revival

faq.question: How is Korean tea culture different from Japanese?
faq.answer: Korean tea culture is generally less formal and ritualistic. Darye emphasizes natural spontaneity and relaxed enjoyment rather than rigid prescribed movements. Korean tea ware tends to be rustic and imperfect, reflecting Buddhist and Confucian aesthetics of humility and simplicity.

faq.question: What happened to Korean tea culture historically?
faq.answer: During the Joseon dynasty, Confucian scholars favored simple living and tea culture declined in favor of alcohol. Japanese colonization further disrupted traditions. Since the 1970s, scholars and monks have actively revived Korean tea culture, reestablishing growing regions and ceremonial practices.
